claims.text: Traditional fusion-welding repair of the targeted heat-sensitive components risks hot cracking because of its high thermal input.
Cold spraying a ceramic-reinforced Ni-alloy composite can repair the damaged surface while imposing low heat input.
Maintaining the substrate well below its melting point results in solid-state deposition.
Avoiding post-deposition stress-relief treatment preserves the low-heat benefit of cold spraying.
Cold spray will produce a densely packed, mechanically bonded coating layer.
The coating will embed hard ceramic particles in the near-surface region.
The resulting composite layer will act as a microstructurally engineered barrier.
The low thermal input of cold spray prevents heat-induced microstructural changes associated with hot cracking.
High-velocity particle impact causes severe plastic deformation at the coating-substrate interface.
Impact-induced plastic deformation promotes mechanical interlocking between the coating and substrate.
Cold spraying produces limited solid-state diffusion at the coating-substrate interface.
Mechanical interlocking, limited solid-state diffusion, and embedded ceramic particles increase surface hardness.
Mechanical interlocking, limited solid-state diffusion, and embedded ceramic particles improve wear resistance.
Mechanical interlocking, limited solid-state diffusion, and embedded ceramic particles improve corrosion resistance.
The cold-sprayed coating will increase surface hardness by approximately 20–40% relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will reduce wear rate relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will improve corrosion resistance relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed repair will avoid hot cracking relative to traditional fusion-welding repair.
The intervention is applicable to heat-sensitive components used in marine, high-salinity, or chemically active environments.
Severe pre-existing substrate damage or environmental aggressiveness beyond the coating's protective capacity may limit effectiveness.
